I am seventy years old. I have farmed these fields in Quzhou since I was a young man, and my father taught me before that. I have only primary schooling, but I know this land and the weather here better than any book.

I have about eight mu of good flat land, the same plot my family has worked for generations. Here on the North China Plain, the only sensible thing is the wheat-maize rotation. I will sow winter wheat in early October after turning the soil with the rotary tiller. I save my own wheat seed every year — it is the improved kind, Luyuan 502, same as my neighbors use. For fertilizer, I spread about 100 jin of compound fertilizer as basal dressing, then top-dress with urea in spring when the wheat greens up. In total that works out to roughly 50 jin of nitrogen, 20 jin of phosphorus, and 7 jin of potassium per mu. I irrigate four times from my well — the young wheat needs it, and spring droughts are common here. I spray three times: herbicide once, and insecticide twice. I expect about 1,000 jin per mu if the weather cooperates. I harvest in early June.

As soon as the wheat comes off, I plant summer maize the same month without extra tillage — there is no time to waste in the double-cropping system. For maize I buy hybrid seed from the shop, Denghai 605, because the yield is reliable and everyone says it is good. I put down less fertilizer than for wheat, around 25 jin nitrogen, 10 jin phosphorus, and 5 jin potassium per mu, mostly compound plus one top-dressing of urea at the jointing stage. Maize does not need as much water as wheat, so I irrigate twice — once if it is dry at sowing, and once at the big trumpet stage. I spray three times to control worms and weeds. I expect around 1,100 jin per mu, and harvest in early October before the cold sets in.

That is my plan. I do not grow cotton or vegetables on a large scale anymore — at my age, two reliable crops are enough, and the wheat-maize rotation feeds my family and leaves some grain to sell.
